spec.text: Right to privacy relating to self-identity is very dear to every human being and well protected under Article 21 of the Constitution. In this context, examine the effect of the amendment in 2026, to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-six. General Studies Paper Two, ten marks, a hundred and fifty words. Privacy and self-identity sit under Article twenty-one. Examine what the twenty twenty-six amendment did to the Transgender Persons Act. Here is the catch. The Act once gave a right to self-perceived identity. Did it survive?

lines.text: In twenty fourteen, in NALSA, the Supreme Court upheld a person's right to decide their own gender.
In twenty seventeen, Puttaswamy quoted NALSA.
Privacy, self-identity and autonomy are fundamental values.

spec.title: Privacy, Self-Identity and the 2026 Transgender Act Amendment

lines.text: So identity now runs through a process.
A medical board must recommend before the District Magistrate issues a certificate.
The definition is a closed list.
Its proviso excludes self-perceived sexual identities.

scenes.vo: So identity now runs through a process. A medical board must recommend before the District Magistrate issues a certificate. The definition is a closed list. Its proviso excludes self-perceived sexual identities. The Act also adds heavier penalties for forcing a transgender identity.

blocks.text: _NALSA_ (2014) and _Puttaswamy_ (2017) place privacy and self-identity within Article 21.

• Act 3 of 2026, in force 25 May 2026, omits s.4(2): the statutory right to _self-perceived gender identity_. • A closed definition; its proviso excludes 'self-perceived sexual identities'. • A _medical board_ must recommend before the District Magistrate issues a certificate. • New penalties for forcing a transgender identity.

• The test: _legality, need, proportionality_ (Chandrachud J.). • NALSA called self-identity a fundamental value; a board's recommendation replaces self-perception. • Puttaswamy called LGBT rights 'real rights'; the proviso is where that reasoning would be tested. • No court has yet ruled on the Act.
So the Act narrows self-identity in statute; whether that passes the _proportionality_ test awaits the courts.

scenes.vo: Section two applies the three tests. Be careful with the last point. No court has ruled on this Act. So the verdict is a reasoned view, not a holding. It says the question awaits the courts.

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It says self-perceived identity stays in section four. It does not. It says the Act began on assent. It began on a notified date. It says the Court struck it down. The record shows no ruling. And it never names the three-fold test.
